chapters.title: International Financial Management and Interest Rate Risk Management
chapters.summary: Appraising overseas projects, raising funds through ADRs, GDRs and other international instruments, and managing interest rate risk with FRAs, swaps, caps and floors.

lesson.heading: International capital budgeting
lesson.body:
Overseas projects add currency risk, country (political) risk, remittance restrictions and different tax regimes. Two consistent methods:

| Method | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| Home currency approach | Forecast foreign currency cash flows, convert at expected spot rates (from IRP or PPP), discount at the home required return |
| Foreign currency approach | Discount foreign cash flows at the foreign-currency equivalent rate, then convert the NPV at today's spot rate |

With parity holding, both give the same NPV. Foreign-equivalent rate = (1 + home rate) x (1 + foreign interest) / (1 + home interest) - 1.

**Parent vs project perspective**: the parent values only the cash it can actually remit (after withholding tax, blocked funds and transfer pricing effects). A project that looks good locally can be unattractive to the parent.

lesson.heading: International sources of finance
lesson.body:
- **ADR (American Depository Receipt)**: a receipt issued by a US depository bank representing shares of a non-US company held by a custodian in the home country; traded in the US in USD.
- **GDR (Global Depository Receipt)**: similar, issued and traded in more than one market (usually Europe: London, Luxembourg).
- **IDR (Indian Depository Receipt)**: issued in India by a foreign company.
- Each receipt represents a fixed number of underlying shares (the conversion ratio). ADR price in ₹ / ratio should be close to the home share price; differences create arbitrage.
- Debt: External Commercial Borrowings (ECB), Euro bonds, Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCB), rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad (masala bonds).

Depository receipts let a company raise foreign equity without listing its shares directly abroad, widen its investor base and gain visibility; the cost is listing and compliance expense and exposure to foreign market sentiment.

lesson.heading: Forward rate agreements (FRA)
lesson.body:
An FRA locks an interest rate for a future period on a notional principal. A **3 x 6 FRA** fixes the rate for a 3-month period starting in 3 months. A borrower buys an FRA to protect against rising rates; a lender sells one.

At the start of the period it is cash-settled on the difference:

**Settlement = [(Reference rate - FRA rate) x Notional x days / 365] / (1 + Reference rate x days / 365)**

The division discounts the interest difference, which relates to the end of the period, back to the settlement date. If the reference rate is above the FRA rate, the FRA buyer receives; if below, the buyer pays. Use 360 days where the question or market convention (for example USD rates) says so.

lesson.heading: Interest rate swaps, caps, floors and collars
lesson.body:
A **plain vanilla swap** exchanges fixed-rate payments for floating-rate payments on a notional principal; only the net amount changes hands.

**Comparative advantage swap**: if two firms have different credit spreads in the fixed and floating markets, each borrows where its advantage is greater and they swap. Total gain = difference in fixed spreads - difference in floating spreads, shared as agreed (less any bank fee).

| Instrument | Protects | Payoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cap | Borrower against rates rising above the cap rate | Pays (Reference - cap) x notional when reference > cap |
| Floor | Lender against rates falling below the floor rate | Pays (floor - Reference) x notional when reference < floor |
| Collar | Borrower: buy cap, sell floor | Premium from floor reduces cost of cap; rate stays within a band |

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Converting all future foreign cash flows at today's spot rate instead of expected future rates.
- Discounting rupee cash flows at a foreign interest rate (or the reverse).
- In FRAs, forgetting to discount the settlement to the start of the period.
- In swap design, computing total gain as the sum instead of the difference of the spread differences.
- Ignoring withholding taxes and remittance limits when valuing from the parent's perspective.

keyPoints: Overseas NPV: convert foreign cash flows at expected spot rates (IRP/PPP) and discount at the home rate.
Foreign-equivalent rate = (1 + home k)(1 + foreign r)/(1 + home r) - 1; both methods give the same NPV.
ADR = US-traded receipt; GDR = traded in several markets (often Europe); IDR = issued in India by a foreign firm.
FRA settlement = (reference - FRA rate) x notional x days/365, discounted at the reference rate.
Swap gain = difference in fixed spreads - difference in floating spreads.
Cap protects borrowers, floor protects lenders, collar = buy cap + sell floor.

cases.title: Case: Himalaya Pharma Ltd US plant
cases.body:
Himalaya Pharma Ltd plans a formulation plant in the US. Cost: USD 10 million, payable now. Expected net cash flows (fully remittable, after all taxes):

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cash flow (USD million) | 4 | 5 | 6 |

The plant has no value after year 3. Spot rate ₹83/USD. Risk-free rates: rupee 8% p.a., USD 4% p.a. Himalaya's required return on rupee cash flows is 14%. Expected future spot rates follow interest rate parity. Round exchange rates and discount factors to 4 decimals.

questions.prompt: Compute the expected spot rate (₹/USD) at the end of year 2 under interest rate parity. Round to 4 decimals.
Compute the NPV of the US plant in rupees. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
If Himalaya instead discounts the USD cash flows directly, which discount rate keeps the result consistent with the rupee approach?
questions.explanation: Foreign-equivalent rate = 1.14 x 1.04 / 1.08 - 1 = 9.78%. Discounting USD flows at this rate and converting the NPV at ₹83 gives the same answer. 10% (14 - 4) is only an approximation.

questions.prompt: From the parent's perspective, which factor would reduce the project's value even if the plant's local NPV is unchanged?
options: A US rule restricting remittance of profits for the first three years
A higher selling price in the US market
A fall in the plant's construction cost
Appreciation of the USD against the rupee
questions.explanation: The parent values only cash it can bring home. Blocked funds delay remittance and lower the parent's NPV; the other options raise value.

questions.prompt: A depository receipt issued by a foreign company to investors in India is called a/an:
questions.explanation: An Indian Depository Receipt (IDR) lets a foreign company raise money from Indian investors. ADRs trade in the US; GDRs in several markets; FCCBs are convertible bonds.

questions.prompt: A company with floating-rate borrowings wants protection if rates rise but wants to benefit if rates fall. It should:
questions.explanation: A cap pays out when rates exceed the cap rate and costs only a premium otherwise, so the borrower keeps the benefit of falling rates. A pay-fixed swap or bought FRA would lock the rate and give up that benefit.

questions.prompt: The buyer of an FRA receives a settlement payment when the reference rate at settlement is above the agreed FRA rate.
questions.explanation: The FRA buyer is protected against rising rates: it effectively pays the FRA rate, so it is compensated when the market rate turns out higher.

questions.prompt: If interest rate parity holds, discounting rupee-converted cash flows at the rupee rate and discounting USD cash flows at the foreign-equivalent rate give different NPVs.
questions.explanation: Under parity the two methods are algebraically identical; differences in an exam answer come only from rounding.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are sources of international finance for an Indian company? (Select all that apply)
options: Indian Depository Receipts issued by the company itself
questions.explanation: IDRs are issued in India by foreign companies, not by Indian companies. The rest are routes for Indian companies to raise funds abroad.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a forward rate agreement covering a 3-month period that starts 3 months from today is called a 3 x ___ FRA.
questions.explanation: The notation is start month x end month: 3 x 6 means the period runs from month 3 to month 6.

questions.prompt: Vidarbha Steel Ltd bought a 3 x 6 FRA at 7.50% on a notional ₹10 crore. On the settlement date the 3-month reference rate is 8.20%. The period is 90 days on a 365-day basis. Compute the settlement amount received by Vidarbha, to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| Step | Working | ₹ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interest difference | (8.20% - 7.50%) x 10,00,00,000 x 90/365 | 1,72,602.74 |
| Discount factor | 1 + 0.082 x 90/365 | 1.020219 |
| **Settlement** | difference / discount factor | **1,69,182** |

questions.prompt: An Indian company's ADR trades at USD 24.60 in New York. One ADR represents 2 equity shares. The exchange rate is ₹83.20/USD. Compute the equivalent rupee price per underlying share, to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: ADR in rupees = 24.60 x 83.20 = ₹2046.72. Per share = 2046.72 / 2 = ₹1023.36. If the share trades well below this in India, arbitrageurs buy shares, convert them into ADRs and sell in the US.

questions.prompt: Design an interest rate swap that benefits both companies equally and show each company's effective cost.
questions.data:
| Company | Fixed rate available | Floating rate available | Wants |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alpha Ltd (AAA) | 7.0% | MIBOR + 0.5% | Floating |
| Beta Ltd (A) | 8.5% | MIBOR + 1.2% | Fixed |

No intermediary is involved.
questions.answer:
| Step | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Difference in fixed rates | 8.5% - 7.0% | 1.5% |
| Difference in floating rates | (MIBOR + 1.2%) - (MIBOR + 0.5%) | 0.7% |
| Total gain from swap | 1.5% - 0.7% | 0.8% |
| Gain to each | 0.8% / 2 | 0.4% |

Alpha has a bigger advantage in fixed (1.5%), so Alpha borrows fixed at 7.0% and Beta borrows floating at MIBOR + 1.2%. Under the swap Alpha pays MIBOR to Beta and Beta pays 6.9% fixed to Alpha.

| Flows | Alpha Ltd | Beta Ltd |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pays to lender | 7.0% | MIBOR + 1.2% |
| Pays under swap | MIBOR | 6.9% |
| Receives under swap | (6.9%) | (MIBOR) |
| **Net cost** | **MIBOR + 0.1%** | **8.1%** |
| Cost without swap | MIBOR + 0.5% | 8.5% |
| Saving | 0.4% | 0.4% |

questions.prompt: Under a swap on a notional ₹50 crore, Kosi Power Ltd pays fixed at 6.80% p.a. and receives 6-month MIBOR. For a half-year in which MIBOR is set at 7.25% p.a., what is the net settlement for that half-year (simple half-year basis)?
questions.explanation: Net = (7.25% - 6.80%) x 50,00,00,000 x 1/2 = ₹11,25,000. Only the net difference is exchanged; the notional never changes hands.

questions.prompt: How does international capital budgeting differ from domestic capital budgeting? Explain the parent versus project perspective.
questions.answer:
- Cash flows arise in foreign currency, so expected exchange rates (from IRP or PPP) are needed to convert them, or a foreign-equivalent discount rate is used.
- Additional risks: exchange rate risk, political and country risk, expropriation, and blocked funds; these are reflected through cash flow adjustments or a higher discount rate.
- Taxes in two countries, withholding taxes on dividends and royalties, and double taxation relief affect the remittable amount.
- Project perspective values all cash flows generated by the subsidiary; parent perspective values only what can be remitted to the parent after taxes and restrictions, including royalties and fees.
- The parent perspective is the correct basis for the investment decision, since shareholders of the parent own only remittable cash.

chapters.title: Corporate Valuation
chapters.summary: Valuing a business with asset, earnings, discounted cash flow and relative approaches, moving from enterprise value to equity value, and measuring value creation with EVA and MVA.

lesson.heading: Approaches to valuation
lesson.body:
| Approach | Method | Suits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asset-based | Net assets at book, replacement or realisable (liquidation) value | Asset-heavy firms, holding companies, liquidation |
| Earnings-based | Future maintainable profit / capitalisation rate | Stable, profitable businesses |
| Cash flow (DCF) | PV of FCFF at WACC (or FCFE at Ke) plus terminal value | Going concerns with forecastable cash flows |
| Relative (market) | Peer multiples: P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales, P/B | Quick checks, listed peers available |

No method is right for every case. Valuers often use more than one and reconcile the results.

lesson.heading: DCF valuation and terminal value
lesson.body:
Steps for an FCFF-based valuation:

- Forecast FCFF for the explicit period (usually 3-10 years).
- Terminal value at the end of the explicit period: **TV = FCFF(n+1) / (WACC - g)**.
- Discount the explicit cash flows and the TV at WACC: this is the **enterprise (firm) value** from operations.
- Add non-operating assets (surplus cash, investments), deduct debt and preference capital to get **equity value**; divide by shares.

The terminal value is often 60-80% of the total, so the long-term growth rate must be realistic (not above long-run nominal GDP growth) and below WACC.

lesson.heading: Enterprise value and relative valuation
lesson.body:
**Enterprise value (EV) = market value of equity + debt + preference capital + minority interest - cash and cash equivalents.**

Worked example (₹ crore):

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Market capitalisation | 1,200 |
| Add: Debt | 350 |
| Add: Preference capital | 50 |
| Less: Cash and equivalents | (100) |
| **Enterprise value** | **1,500** |

Equity multiples (P/E, P/B) are applied to equity measures (EPS, book value). Enterprise multiples (EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales) are applied to pre-interest measures and give EV, from which net debt is deducted. EV/EBITDA is preferred when peers have different leverage or depreciation policies.

lesson.heading: Economic Value Added and Market Value Added
lesson.body:
**EVA = NOPAT - (WACC x capital employed)**, where NOPAT = EBIT x (1 - tax rate). A positive EVA means the business earned more than the cost of all the capital it used.

**MVA = market value of the firm (equity + debt) - capital employed.** MVA is the market's view of the PV of all future EVAs.

EVA is used for performance measurement and incentive pay, because it charges managers for the capital they tie up. Adjustments are often made to accounting figures (capitalising R&D, removing non-recurring items).

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Using FCFF(n) instead of FCFF(n+1) in the terminal value formula.
- Discounting the terminal value for n+1 years: it is a value at the end of year n, so discount for n years.
- Forgetting to add surplus cash or to deduct debt when moving from enterprise to equity value.
- Applying EV/EBITDA to get equity value directly.
- Deducting interest when computing NOPAT for EVA: interest is covered by the capital charge.

keyPoints: Approaches: asset-based, earnings capitalisation, DCF, relative multiples.
TV = FCFF(n+1)/(WACC - g), discounted for n years.
Equity value = enterprise value + surplus cash - debt - preference capital.
EV = market cap + debt + preference + minority - cash.
EVA = NOPAT - WACC x capital employed; MVA = market value - capital employed.
Use equity multiples with equity measures and EV multiples with pre-interest measures.

cases.title: Case: Tapti Retail Ltd valuation
cases.body:
Ojas Capital is advising a private equity fund on a stake in Tapti Retail Ltd. The forecast free cash flows to the firm are:

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FCFF (₹ crore) | 120 | 140 | 160 |

After year 3, FCFF will grow at 5% a year forever. WACC is 12%. Tapti has debt of ₹400 crore and surplus cash of ₹60 crore. It has 20 crore equity shares. Use discount factors: year 1 = 0.8929, year 2 = 0.7972, year 3 = 0.7118.

questions.prompt: Compute the terminal value of Tapti at the end of year 3, in ₹ crore.
Compute the value per equity share of Tapti. Round to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Working | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PV of FCFF year 1 | 120 x 0.8929 | 107.1480 |
| PV of FCFF year 2 | 140 x 0.7972 | 111.6080 |
| PV of FCFF year 3 | 160 x 0.7118 | 113.8880 |
| PV of terminal value | 2,400 x 0.7118 | 1708.3200 |
| Enterprise value |  | 2040.9640 |
| Less: Debt |  | (400.00) |
| Add: Surplus cash |  | 60.00 |
| Equity value |  | 1700.9640 |
| **Per share** | / 20 crore shares | **₹85.05** |

questions.prompt: Tapti's shares are being offered to the fund at ₹80 each. Based on the DCF value, the offer price is:
options: Not comparable, because DCF gives enterprise value only
questions.explanation: Intrinsic value is about ₹85.05 per share, above the ₹80 offer, so the offer is attractive (a margin of safety exists). Equity value already adjusts for debt and cash, so the comparison is valid.

questions.prompt: What share of Tapti's enterprise value comes from the terminal value?
questions.explanation: PV of TV = ₹1708.32 crore out of EV ₹2040.96 crore = 83.7%. This is why the long-term growth and WACC assumptions need the most scrutiny.

questions.prompt: A company's future maintainable profit after tax is ₹50 crore and the normal capitalisation rate for the industry is 12.5%. Its value under the earnings capitalisation method is:
questions.explanation: Value = maintainable profit / capitalisation rate = 50 / 0.125 = ₹400 crore.

questions.prompt: Which item is deducted when computing enterprise value from market capitalisation?
questions.explanation: EV = market cap + debt + preference + minority interest - cash. Cash is deducted because an acquirer of the whole firm effectively gets it back.

questions.prompt: A company with positive accounting profit always has a positive EVA.
questions.explanation: Accounting profit ignores the cost of equity. If NOPAT is less than WACC x capital employed, EVA is negative even though the company reports a profit.

questions.prompt: EV/EBITDA is less affected than P/E by differences in capital structure between the company and its peers.
questions.explanation: EBITDA is before interest and EV includes debt, so leverage differences largely cancel out. P/E uses earnings after interest and is distorted by leverage.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are correct pairings of a multiple with the value it produces? (Select all that apply)
options: P/E x EPS gives value per share
EV/EBITDA x EBITDA gives enterprise value
P/B x book value per share gives value per share
EV/Sales x sales gives equity value directly
P/E x EBITDA gives enterprise value
questions.explanation: Equity multiples applied to equity measures give equity value; EV multiples applied to pre-interest measures give EV, from which net debt must be deducted. EV/Sales gives EV, not equity value; P/E cannot be applied to EBITDA.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: market value of the firm minus capital employed is called ___ (abbreviation).
questions.explanation: MVA measures the value the market believes management has added over the capital invested; it equals the PV of expected future EVAs.

questions.prompt: A listed peer group trades at 9x EV/EBITDA. Godavari Foods Ltd has EBITDA of ₹150 crore, debt of ₹300 crore, cash of ₹50 crore and 10 crore shares. Compute its value per share using this multiple.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| EV = 9 x 150 | 1,350 |
| Less: Debt | (300) |
| Add: Cash | 50 |
| Equity value | 1,100 |
| **Per share (/ 10 crore)** | **₹110.00** |

questions.prompt: A division has NOPAT of ₹84 crore, capital employed of ₹600 crore and a WACC of 11%. Compute its EVA in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation: Capital charge = 600 x 11% = ₹66 crore. EVA = 84 - 66 = ₹18.00 crore.

questions.prompt: Compute (a) WACC, (b) NOPAT, (c) EVA and (d) MVA of Mahanadi Cables Ltd and comment.
questions.data:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| EBIT | 300 |
| Equity capital employed (book) | 900 |
| Debt (book = market) | 600 |
| Market capitalisation | 1,400 |

Tax rate 25%. Cost of equity 15%. Pre-tax cost of debt 10%. Use book value weights for WACC.
questions.answer:
| Step | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capital employed | 900 + 600 | ₹1,500 crore |
| (a) WACC | (900/1,500 x 15%) + (600/1,500 x 10% x 0.75) | 12.00% |
| (b) NOPAT | 300 x (1 - 0.25) | ₹225.00 crore |
| Capital charge | 1,500 x 12.00% | ₹180.00 crore |
| (c) **EVA** | 225.00 - 180.00 | **₹45.00 crore** |
| (d) **MVA** | (1,400 + 600) - 1,500 | **₹500.00 crore** |

Positive EVA shows the company earned more than its cost of capital this year. Positive MVA shows the market expects it to keep creating value.

questions.prompt: Explain the DCF approach to corporate valuation and the role of terminal value.
questions.answer:
- Value = PV of expected free cash flows; FCFF is discounted at WACC to give enterprise value (FCFE at Ke gives equity value directly).
- Forecast FCFF = EBIT(1 - t) + depreciation - capex - increase in working capital for an explicit period.
- Terminal value captures cash flows after the explicit period, usually by the Gordon growth formula FCFF(n+1)/(WACC - g) or an exit multiple.
- TV often forms most of the value, so g must be sustainable and below WACC; small changes in g or WACC move the value sharply, so sensitivity analysis is essential.
- Equity value = EV + non-operating assets - debt - preference capital - minority interest; divide by shares for value per share.

questions.prompt: What is Economic Value Added? Why is it preferred to accounting profit for measuring performance?
questions.answer:
- EVA = NOPAT - WACC x capital employed: profit left after charging for all capital, debt and equity.
- Accounting profit charges only interest, not the cost of equity, so a profitable firm can still destroy value.
- EVA makes managers accountable for capital used: they create value by raising returns, investing only where return exceeds WACC, or releasing unproductive capital.
- It links to MVA (PV of future EVAs) and so to shareholder wealth, and is used in incentive schemes.
- Limitations: accounting adjustments are subjective, it is a single-period measure and can discourage long-gestation investments.

chapters.title: Mergers, Acquisitions, Corporate Restructuring and Startup Finance
chapters.summary: Types of combinations and restructuring, swap ratios and post-merger EPS and price, synergy and cost of acquisition, and how startups are financed and valued.

lesson.heading: Mergers, acquisitions and restructuring
lesson.body:
| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Horizontal merger | Firms in the same line of business (economies of scale, market share) |
| Vertical merger | Firms at different stages of the same value chain (supplier or customer) |
| Conglomerate merger | Unrelated businesses (diversification) |
| Congeneric merger | Related but not identical businesses sharing technology or customers |
| Reverse merger | A smaller or loss-making firm absorbs a larger or profitable one, or an unlisted company merges into a listed shell |

Restructuring also includes **demerger** (spin-off of a division into a new company owned by the same shareholders), **divestiture / slump sale** (sale of a business for a lump sum), **buy-back**, **leveraged buy-out (LBO)** and **management buy-out (MBO)**, and **equity carve-out** (IPO of a minority stake in a subsidiary).

The rationale is **synergy**: value of combined firm > sum of stand-alone values, from cost savings, revenue gains, tax benefits or a lower cost of capital.

lesson.heading: Swap ratio and post-merger EPS
lesson.body:
**Swap (exchange) ratio** = shares of the acquirer issued for each share of the target. Bases: EPS, market price, book value, intrinsic (DCF) value, or a weighted mix.

- Swap ratio (basis X) = target's X per share / acquirer's X per share
- Post-merger EPS = (EA + EB + synergy earnings) / (NA + NB x swap ratio)
- Target shareholders' equivalent EPS = post-merger EPS x swap ratio
- Maximum swap ratio with no dilution of acquirer's EPS: shares issued = (EA + EB) / EPS of A - NA
- Post-merger market price = post-merger P/E x post-merger EPS

Worked example: A earns ₹40 crore on 8 crore shares (EPS ₹5); B earns ₹12 crore on 4 crore shares (EPS ₹3). EPS-based swap ratio = 3/5 = 0.6.

| Particulars | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shares issued to B | 4 x 0.6 | 2.4 crore |
| Post-merger EPS | (40 + 12) / (8 + 2.4) | ₹5.00 |

With an EPS-based ratio and no synergy, neither side's EPS changes. Any other basis transfers EPS from one group of shareholders to the other.

lesson.heading: Synergy, cost of acquisition and NPV to the acquirer
lesson.body:
- **Synergy** = V(AB) - [V(A) + V(B)]
- **Cost of acquisition** = cash paid, or (shares issued x post-merger share price) when paid in shares
- **Premium** = cost - V(B)
- **NPV to acquirer** = synergy - premium = [V(B) + synergy] - cost

When payment is in shares, target shareholders share in the synergy (and any overpayment), so the true cost depends on the post-merger price, not the pre-merger price.

lesson.heading: Startup finance
lesson.body:
| Stage | Typical source |
| --- | --- |
| Idea / pre-seed | Bootstrapping (founders' savings), friends and family, grants, incubators |
| Seed | Angel investors, angel networks, accelerators, crowdfunding |
| Early stage (Series A, B) | Venture capital funds |
| Growth / pre-IPO | Later-stage VC, private equity, venture debt |
| Exit | IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale to another fund |

**VC method of valuation**: estimate exit (terminal) value in year n, then:

- Post-money value today = exit value / (1 + target return)^n
- Required ownership = investment / post-money value
- Pre-money value = post-money value - investment

A **pitch deck** covers the problem, solution, market size, business model, traction, competition, team, financials and the ask (amount and use of funds). Investors also negotiate terms such as liquidation preference, anti-dilution protection, board seats and vesting of founders' shares.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Inverting the swap ratio: it is target's value per share / acquirer's value per share.
- Using the pre-merger price of the acquirer to value shares issued; the cost depends on the post-merger price.
- Forgetting to add synergy earnings to combined earnings when the question gives them.
- Confusing pre-money and post-money value in the VC method.
- Assuming the post-merger P/E equals the acquirer's P/E unless the question says so.

keyPoints: Swap ratio = target value per share / acquirer value per share (EPS, MPS, book or intrinsic basis).
Post-merger EPS = (EA + EB + synergy) / (NA + NB x ER); target's equivalent EPS = post-merger EPS x ER.
Maximum ER without EPS dilution: shares issued = (EA + EB)/EPS(A) - NA.
NPV to acquirer = V(B) + synergy - cost of acquisition; share-based cost uses post-merger price.
Restructuring: demerger, slump sale, buy-back, LBO, MBO, equity carve-out.
VC method: post-money = exit value/(1 + r)^n; ownership = investment/post-money; pre-money = post - investment.

cases.title: Case: Amber Ltd acquires Bharat Ltd
cases.body:
Amber Ltd, a listed paints company, has agreed to absorb Bharat Ltd, a smaller listed competitor. Pre-merger data:

| Particulars | Amber Ltd | Bharat Ltd |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earnings after tax (₹ crore) | 60 | 15 |
| Number of equity shares (crore) | 10 | 5 |
| Market price per share (₹) | 120 | 45 |

The boards propose a share exchange based on market prices. No synergy in earnings is expected in the first year. Analysts expect the merged company to trade at a P/E of 18.

questions.prompt: What swap ratio results from the market price basis?
options: 0.375 Amber share for each Bharat share
0.500 Amber share for each Bharat share
2.667 Amber shares for each Bharat share
0.750 Amber share for each Bharat share
questions.explanation: Swap ratio = 45 / 120 = 0.375. Amber issues 5 x 0.375 = 1.875 crore shares. 0.500 is the EPS-based ratio (3/6); 2.667 inverts the ratio.

questions.prompt: Compute Amber's EPS after the merger. Round to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Combined earnings | 60 + 15 | ₹75 crore |
| Shares after merger | 10 + 5 x 0.375 | 11.875 crore |
| **Post-merger EPS** | 75 / 11.875 | **₹6.32** |

questions.prompt: Compute the maximum swap ratio Amber can offer without diluting its pre-merger EPS. Round to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Amber's EPS = 60/10 = ₹6. To keep EPS at ₹6 on ₹75 crore earnings, total shares can be 75/6 = 12.5 crore, so at most 2.5 crore new shares for 5 crore Bharat shares: ratio = 0.50.

questions.prompt: What happens to the EPS of Bharat's shareholders on an equivalent basis?
questions.explanation: Equivalent EPS = 6.3158 x 0.375 = ₹2.37. Bharat's P/E (15) is below Amber's (20), so a market-price ratio gives Bharat fewer shares than an EPS ratio would; Amber's EPS rises and Bharat's equivalent EPS falls.

questions.prompt: If the merged company trades at a P/E of 18, what is the expected market price of an Amber share after the merger?
questions.explanation: Price = P/E x EPS = 18 x 6.3158 = ₹113.68. This is below Amber's ₹120 pre-merger price: the market is not rewarding the EPS rise because the combined P/E falls.

questions.prompt: A company transfers its cement division to a new company, and the shareholders of the original company receive shares of the new company in proportion to their holdings. This is a:
questions.explanation: In a demerger the division moves to a resulting company and the same shareholders get its shares. In a slump sale the business is sold for a lump-sum consideration paid to the company.

questions.prompt: When the swap ratio is based on EPS and there is no synergy, the EPS of both groups of shareholders is unchanged after the merger.
questions.explanation: An EPS-based ratio issues shares exactly in proportion to earnings contributed, so post-merger EPS equals the acquirer's EPS and the target's equivalent EPS equals its old EPS.

questions.prompt: In the VC method, pre-money valuation equals post-money valuation plus the amount invested.
questions.explanation: Post-money = pre-money + investment. Pre-money is therefore post-money minus the investment.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are sources of synergy in a merger? (Select all that apply)
options: Economies of scale in production and distribution
Use of accumulated tax losses of one firm against profits of the other, where permitted
Lower combined cost of capital from greater size and stability
Higher EPS created only by issuing shares at a high P/E
questions.explanation: Operating, revenue, tax and financial synergies create real value. EPS 'bootstrapping' from P/E differences does not add cash flows, so it is not true synergy.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: acquisition of a company largely funded by debt secured on the target's own assets and cash flows is called a ___ buy-out.
questions.explanation: In an LBO the target's cash flows service the acquisition debt; high leverage magnifies equity returns and risk.

questions.prompt: A VC fund is asked to invest ₹10 crore in Kshitij Robotics Pvt Ltd. It expects the company to be worth ₹200 crore at exit in 5 years and targets a return of 40% p.a. Compute the percentage stake the fund should require. Answer as a % to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Step | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Post-money value | 200 / (1.40)^5 = 200 / 5.37824 | ₹37.1869 crore |
| Required stake | 10 / 37.1869 | 26.89% |
| Pre-money value | 37.1869 - 10 | ₹27.1869 crore |

questions.prompt: Evaluate the acquisition of Tara Ltd by Sitara Ltd under (a) payment in shares and (b) payment in cash.
questions.data:
| Particulars | Sitara Ltd | Tara Ltd |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number of shares (crore) | 20 | 5 |
| Market price per share (₹) | 25 | 20 |

The merger is expected to create synergy of ₹40 crore. Option (a): Sitara issues 5 crore new shares (1 for 1). Option (b): Sitara pays ₹125 crore in cash.
questions.answer:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Value of Sitara (20 x 25) | 500 |
| Value of Tara (5 x 20) | 100 |
| Synergy | 40 |
| Value of combined firm (before payment) | 640 |

**(a) Payment in shares**

| Step | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shares after merger | 20 + 5 | 25 crore |
| Post-merger price | 640 / 25 | ₹25.60 |
| Cost of acquisition | 5 x 25.60 | ₹128.00 crore |
| NPV to Sitara | (100 + 40) - 128.00 | ₹12.00 crore |
| Gain to Tara's shareholders | 128.00 - 100 | ₹28.00 crore |

**(b) Payment in cash**

| Step | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost of acquisition |  | ₹125.00 crore |
| NPV to Sitara | (100 + 40) - 125.00 | ₹15.00 crore |
| Gain to Tara's shareholders | 125.00 - 100 | ₹25.00 crore |

Cash gives Sitara the higher NPV (₹15.00 crore vs ₹12.00 crore) because in a share deal Tara's shareholders receive 20% of the combined firm, including a share of the synergy. In both cases total gain = ₹40 crore. A share deal is still preferable if Sitara is unsure about the synergy, since Tara's holders then share that risk.

questions.prompt: Explain the bases on which a swap ratio can be determined and the limitations of each.
questions.answer:
- EPS basis: ratio of EPS; ignores growth, quality of earnings and market perception, and differing accounting policies.
- Market price basis: reflects investor expectations, but prices can be volatile, manipulated or thinly traded.
- Book value (net asset) basis: objective, but historical costs ignore earning power and intangibles.
- Intrinsic value (DCF) basis: theoretically the best because it uses future cash flows, but depends heavily on assumptions.
- In practice a weighted average of several bases is negotiated, supported by a registered valuer's report and a fairness opinion; the swap ratio decides how synergy is shared between the two groups of shareholders.

questions.prompt: Describe the sources of finance available to a startup at different stages and how a venture capitalist values a startup.
questions.answer:
- Pre-seed: bootstrapping, friends and family, government grants and incubators.
- Seed: angel investors and angel networks, accelerators, crowdfunding.
- Early and growth stages: venture capital (Series A, B, C), venture debt, private equity; exits through IPO, strategic sale or secondary sale.
- VC method: estimate exit value in year n (often a multiple of expected earnings or revenue), discount at a high target return (30-60%) to get post-money value, required ownership = investment / post-money, pre-money = post-money - investment.
- High target returns reflect the high failure rate; term sheets add protection through liquidation preference, anti-dilution clauses, board seats and founder vesting.
